message.content:
Here are five flower species that play a prominent role in pollination across South America—each with its own unique pollinator relationships:

| # | Flower Species | Native Range | Typical Pollinators | Why It Matters |
|---|----------------|--------------|---------------------|----------------|
| 1 | **Heliconia rostrata** (Hummingbird‑flower) | Tropical rainforests of Central & South America | Hummingbirds (especially *Selasphorus* spp.) | Its bright, banana‑shaped bracts attract hummingbirds, making it a key nectar source in lowland forests. |
| 2 | **Passiflora edulis** (Passionfruit) | Andes & Amazon basin | Bees, butterflies, and some bats | Provides high‑protein pollen and nectar; its complex floral structure has evolved to accommodate diverse pollinators. |
| 3 | **Anthurium andraeanum** (Flamingo Lily) | Amazon rainforest | Beetles (primarily *Melolontha* spp.) | A classic beetle‑pollinated flower; its spadix emits heat and scent to lure beetles into the reproductive zone. |
| 4 | **Cattleya labiata** (Pink Cattleya) | Andean cloud forests | Bees (mainly *Bombus* spp.) | One of the most celebrated orchids in cultivation; its labellum guides bees to the pollinia, ensuring cross‑pollination. |
| 5 | **Erythrina crista‑galli** (Cockspur Thorn) | Atlantic Forest & Cerrado | Bees, especially *Xylocopa* spp. | Its bright red flowers are a major food source for large carpenter bees, which also help disperse seeds via their pollen loads. |

These species illustrate the diversity of pollination strategies—from hummingbird‑mediated nectar feeding to beetle‑attracted heat and scent—to the intricate dance between plants and insects that sustains South American ecosystems.
